adj1.description: Build descriptors with specifiers and subordinate clauses

mixPrep.description: Mix different prepositional types via coordination

noun1.description: Build nouns with descriptors and subordinate clauses

rules.note: Example: cats and dogs -> COORD becomes NOUN

quant1.description: M50 QUANTIFIER_SUBJECT: promote a bare quantifier/numeral (this/both/each/all/most/one..ten, tagged SubType.QUANTIFIER regardless of which POS it landed on) to a standalone NOUN when it is used pronominally instead of as a determiner. Runs right after noun1/noun2 -- ordinary determiner-attachment ('both teams', 'this dog') has already had its chance to consume the quantifier as a 'before' DESCRIPTOR of a following noun, so if it is STILL unconsumed here, nothing claimed it as a modifier and it is standing alone ('both were...', 'each of the four...', 'this would help...', 'three were doubles'). Runs before normPP1/noun3 so a partitive PP ('of the four wayward shots') can still attach to the promoted NOUN exactly like any other noun -- no new rule needed for the partitive shape. Two rules because the closed-class/lexicon tag for these words lands on either DESCRIPTOR (DET/ADJ) or SPECIFIER (ADV) depending on the word; both convert the same way. Deliberately NOT a tag-lattice branch (see pos_tagger.py WORD_SUBTYPES comment) -- this is a single deterministic transform, so it can never be pruned away by ParserConfig.max_hypotheses the way an added POS-ambiguity branch could.

rules.note: Bare quantifier/numeral, DET/ADJ reading: 'both were...', 'three were doubles'
Bare quantifier, ADV reading: 'each of the four...', 'most was quiet'

question1.description: Subject-initial questions: grab the postposed bare NOMINAL as SUBJECT before predicate1's generic transitive-object rule (VERBAL+NOMINAL(after)->OBJECT) or noun3's NP-internal PP attachment ever see it. Runs before aux1 (anchor is still the tagger's raw MODIFIER, subtypes still carry PROGRESSIVE from the copula word list) and before noun3/normPP1's NP-attachment, so it never competes with either -- it simply claims the subject first. Two DISJOINT shapes, kept apart deliberately (M43: the wh-cleft's verb1/rel2 collision showed unscoped SPECIFIER-adjacency rules misfire on relative/wh material, so both rules here are scoped as tightly as possible: RELATIVE subtype for the wh-word, sentence-initial position_constraints for the inversion, neither touches verb1/rel2 at all).

rules.note: Wh-question: 'where is the ball ?' -- English fronts the wh-word, so the copula has no subject to its left. Scoped to RELATIVE-tagged wh-adverbs (where/when/why/how) only, so verb1's ordinary adverb-adjacency rules ('quickly runs') are never touched; sentence-initial position_constraints so it can never fire on a mid-sentence 'where' (e.g. a future embedded question).

Yes/no subject-aux inversion: 'is the ball in the garden ?' -- the copula is fronted with no subject before it. Scoped to sentence-initial copula only (position_constraints), so an ordinary mid-sentence copula ('mary is happy') is never touched.

exist1.description: M50 bonus, EXISTENTIAL_THERE: 'there is a problem', 'there was n't a bit of trouble'. Without this, predicate1's generic copula-object rules grab the postposed logical subject as an OBJECT/INDIRECT_OBJECT of the copula, and expletive 'there' itself gets attached as an ordinary adverbial SPECIFICATION -- no SUBJECT edge ever forms. Scoped exactly like question1's inversion rule: 'there' must carry the EXISTENTIAL subtype (pos_tagger.py; ordinary locative 'there' -- 'he went there' -- is unaffected since it never sits sentence-initial immediately before a copula) AND sit at position 0 (position_constraints), and the anchor must still be the tagger's raw copula MODIFIER (runs in the same slot as question1, before aux1/verb1/predicate1 ever transform it). Three rules for how much sits between the copula and the logical subject: nothing, one adverb ('definitely'), or a negation particle ('n't') -- the DSL's before/after elements always require at least one match, so each gap width needs its own rule. Jumps straight to CLAUSE (not PREDICATE) so clause1 never re-fires on the same anchor looking for a preverbal NOMINAL that isn't there.

rules.note: 'there is a problem' -- subject directly after the copula
'there is definitely some ligament damage' -- one adverb between copula and subject
'there was n't a bit of trouble' -- negation particle between copula and subject
Example: on table and under chair

Infinitive: to run, to see (anchor becomes NOMINAL result). Scoped to INFINITIVE (round 2): without it, any MODIFIER (e.g. a modal like "can") immediately before an already-VERBAL node was wrongly read as an infinitive marker, stealing SUBJECT binding in modal+passive chains like "can be found".
Gerund as nominal: running is fun (PARTICIPLE → NOMINAL)
Participle as adjective: running water (PARTICIPLE → DESCRIPTOR)

Negation: not run, n't go. Scoped to NEGATIVE (round 2): without it, any MODIFIER (e.g. "be"/"is") immediately before a VERBAL was wrongly consumed as if it were a negation particle, pre-empting aux1 for modal+passive chains like "can be found".

rel1.description: Relative clauses with pronouns (fires before clause1 so the relative pronoun is still unconsumed)

rules.note: Relative clause: the dog who chased (anchor->PREDICATE, PREDICATE->who)

Object-relative clause: the ball that mary found (gap after the verb -- the relative marker is not the embedded subject, so the intervening NOMINAL is; anchor stays NOMINAL so it can still become the matrix clause's own subject)

rel2.description: Relative clauses with adverbs (fires before clause1)

rules.note: Relative adverb: the place where I live

noun4.description: Noun-noun apposition (placed after rel1/rel2 so relative pronouns are not consumed first)

rules.note: Noun-noun apposition (late-binding, after relative clause rules)

appositive1.description: M50 appositive/parenthetical gap-skip: a bracketed span (comma-set, dash-set, or paren-set) sitting between a subject NOMINAL and its predicate defeats clause1's strict adjacency requirement (before[0] search stops at the first unconsumed, non-matching node). Consuming the bracketed span here -- attaching its content as a MODIFICATION on the head NOMINAL -- lets clause1's leftward search skip straight past it (search_direction skips CONSUMED nodes even under a 'one' quantifier) and find the real subject. Runs after rel1/rel2/noun4 so an appositive with its own relative clause ('the quarterback who led the eagles...') is already folded into a single NOMINAL before this rule ever looks at it; runs before clause1 so the gap is gone by the time SUBJECT-attachment is tried. Two content shapes per bracket kind: a NOMINAL appositive ('the league commissioner') and a bare parenthetical adverb ('however'). Punctuation is disambiguated via the M50 COMMA/DASH/PAREN_OPEN/PAREN_CLOSE subtypes (pos_tagger.py WORD_SUBTYPES) so this never matches an ordinary sentence-final period or unrelated NIL.

rules.note: Comma-set appositive: 'pete rozelle , the league commissioner , pointed out'

Comma-set appositive, two-word compound-noun head ('the league commissioner', 'sports editor of the globe-democrat'): nominal1 promotes NOUN->NOMINAL long before any noun-noun apposition rule runs, so an unmodified two-word compound never collapses to the single NOMINAL the rule above expects. Scoped strictly inside the comma pair (both NOMINALs must sit between the two COMMA-tagged NILs), so this never runs on an ordinary two-item subject list elsewhere in the sentence.
Dash-set appositive: 'the leaders - texas - made a dent'
Paren-set appositive: 'bill white ( sore ankles ) should be ready'

aux1.description: Auxiliary verbs modify main verbs (modals, perfect, progressive, passive)

rules.note: Passive voice: be + past participle (mary can be found). Anchor is the participle (not "be") so push_subtypes lands on the node that survives the aux1 chain; SUBJECT still comes from the generic clause1 rule (preverbal NOMINAL -> SUBJECT), so no ConnectionType change is needed downstream.
Modal + verb: can run, should go
Perfect auxiliary + verb: has run, had eaten
Progressive auxiliary + verb: is running, was walking
Bare progressive copula -> VERBAL (e.g. 'is' in 'mary is in the kitchen')

quote1.description: M50 quote-inversion: postposed subject of a quotation's reporting verb (quote-close , said long jim .). Without this, predicate1's generic VERBAL+NOMINAL(after)->OBJECT rule grabs the speaker as a direct object of 'said'. Scoped to a directly-preceding quote-close token ('''', 1 or 2 positions back, skipping at most one intervening punctuation mark such as comma/!/?) so ordinary transitive verbs elsewhere in the sentence are never touched -- the quote-close subtype only exists on the literal '''' token. Runs before predicate1 (claims the VERBAL anchor first, exactly like question1's subject-aux-inversion rules) and jumps straight to CLAUSE (not PREDICATE) so clause1's generic preverbal-NOMINAL rule never re-fires on the same anchor and adds a second, spurious SUBJECT from something unconsumed further left (e.g. a NOMINAL still sitting inside the quoted material).

rules.note: Quote-close, one punctuation mark, reporting verb, subject: quote-close , said long jim .
Quote-close directly adjacent to the reporting verb, no intervening punctuation: quote-close said ratcliff
Example: dog runs and cat sleeps

verb1b.description: Second-pass: attach subordinate clauses to already-formed CLAUSEs (matrix verbs)

rules.note: Second pass: [john said] + [that he left](SUBORDINATE) -> CLAUSE
